document1: Allocating a lump-sum or periodic pension

example_shared_block: While the intent of all pension plans is to pay a pension benefit when an employee retires, sometimes the employment ends before the employee reaches retirement age. If the employee has worked a certain amount of time according to the provisions of the plan, the contributions are non-refundable and locked in until retirement age. If the employee leaves the employment for any reason before the contributions are locked in, the contributions and interest are paid to the employee on termination of the employment. When termination of employment before the normal age of retirement or early retirement occurs, clients may receive a return of their contributions on separation from the employment. As pensions can be funded by either the employer or employee or both, how the return of contributions is treated for benefit purposes depends on whether the employee or the employer made the contributions.

document1: Allocating a lump-sum or periodic pension
document2: Modifying the allocation of a lump-sum or periodic pension
example_shared_block: While the intent of all pension plans is to pay a pension benefit when an employee retires, sometimes the employment ends before the employee reaches retirement age. If the employee has worked a certain amount of time according to the provisions of the plan, the contributions are non-refundable and locked in until retirement age. If the employee leaves the employment for any reason before the contributions are locked in, the contributions and interest are paid to the employee on termination of the employment. When termination of employment before the normal age of retirement or early retirement occurs, clients may receive a return of their contributions on separation from the employment. As pensions can be funded by either the employer or employee or both, how the return of contributions is treated for benefit purposes depends on whether the employee or the employer made the contributions.

document2: Converting an active EI claim to MPS due to third party fraud — IPOC
example_shared_block: When payments are fraudulently received, the third party is responsible for the resulting OP. Integrity refers the case to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and follows up to establish the OP on the third party’s file, if necessary. No further action is required from the processing officer related to the third party’s OP until the third party is identified. If the third party is known, the IPOC officer refers the file to a Business Expertise Advisor for guidance.

document1: Converting a terminated EI claim to MPS due to third party fraud — IPOC
document2: Converting an active EI claim to MPS due to third party fraud — IPOC
example_shared_block: If a client is a Quebec resident, the IPOC officer determines the federal and Quebec provincial taxes when adjusting the client’s tax file. When weeks were paid to the third party in the current tax year and they must be removed or cancelled from the client’s file, the IPOC officer reviews the Payment Summary (MN19) screen in FTS for a detailed breakdown of the taxes. When requesting an amended T4E, if the third party received fraudulent payments in a previous tax year, the IPOC officer reviews the weeks paid to the third party by selecting the tax year on the Statement of benefits paid (T4E) screen. The officer then selects the Itemized Statement link for a breakdown of the taxes.

example_shared_block: The agent manually registers claims that are not automated in ACP. Training is not automatically adjudicated on manually registered claims. Instead, ACP assigns an Adjudication Issue (ADJ) WI to an agent because it could not automate the decision. Adjudication of these training ADJ WIs is required , and the agent follows the appropriate procedures to resolve them. Even if ACP initially allowed training, when a training ADJ WI is assigned (e.g. upon renewal), the agent must adjudicate. Additionally, if it is determined that a disentitlement applies from the start date of the training course, the Level 2 agent imposes a retroactive D3.

example_shared_block: Pensions that are paid based on contributions to a plan by the employer, the client or both are earnings for benefits purposes. Pension payments are linked to the client’s employment because the employment made the pension payments possible. This is true whether the monies are paid in a lump-sum or whether they are paid on a periodic basis (annuity), and regardless of what the client chooses to do with the monies. Pension payments from the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) or other provisional plans are also paid based on contributions made by the client while working for an employer and are also considered earnings for benefit purposes.

For EI purposes, pension credits paid as an annuity are referred to as a periodic pension. Many employers’ pension plans, the CPP and the Quebec Pension Plan are paid as an annuity.

example_shared_block: Only one ROE can be matched to each period of employment listed in NWS. The agent must review the Search / Correct - Results screen in RCM to determine if the ROE in the ROE RFS Action WI is the one with the last day for which paid (LDP) closest to the last day worked (LDW) for one of the periods of employment. The agent creates a link between the ROE and the period of employment with the matching employer’s name and best match for LDP and LDW. If either the employer’s name does not match or the LDP and LDW are not a good match, the agent does not create a link between the ROE and the period of employment.

example_shared_block: The officer manually registers claims that are not automated in ACP. Training is not automatically adjudicated on manually registered claims. Instead, ACP assigns an Adjudication Issue (ADJ) WI to an officer because it could not automate the decision. Adjudication of these training ADJ WIs is required , and the officer follows the appropriate procedures to resolve them. Even if ACP initially allowed training, when a training ADJ WI is assigned (e.g. upon renewal), the officer must adjudicate. Additionally, if it is determined that a disentitlement applies from the start date of the training course, the Level 2 officer imposes a retroactive D3.

example_shared_block: Fraudulent paper ROEs were created without the knowledge of the true SIN-holder and the employer associated with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) business number (BN) indicated in block 5 of the ROE. There are also instances where there are reasons to suspect that the business identified on the ROE is illegitimate or suspicious and was created to issue fraudulent ROEs. These fraudulent ROEs were sent to Service Canada and scanned as documents in support of fraudulent applications for benefits, or uploaded in AW or MSCA. A close examination may reveal a difference in the font and size of the characters in the serial number of these ROEs when compared to the normal format. In some cases, RCM validates the serial number and does not signal the ROE as a duplicate, because that serial number was used to establish an EI claim more than 11 years ago. In other situations, the serial number has been issued within the last 11 years to a different business number than the one used on the fraudulent ROE, however, RCM validates the serial number but does not flag it as a duplicate because the ROE was never used to establish an EI claim.

Both the BE Memo and the Digest explain that, under FCA A-29-22 , when adjudicating availability, the officer must consider the clients’ work history while attending training, in addition to other factors (i.e. the number of hours clients are attending training). Clients can rebut the presumption of non-availability if they can demonstrate having a regular work history outside of the training hours while taking full-time training. Using any previous ROEs, the officer reviews the number of hours the client worked while attending training to determine if the client can rebut the presumption of non-availability. Clients must also demonstrate a willingness and ability to remain available for a similar work schedule. Clients must not reduce or restrict their available hours of work beyond what is reasonable, given their work history, while attending training. example_shared_block: An ADJ WI is created for every new contentious issue. When opening an ADJ WI, the officer must always check to see if there is a Resolve Issue tab. If there is a Resolve Issue tab, the officer can document the decision directly in the ADJ WI by completing all mandatory screens. When the ADJ WI is completed, NWS creates a ROD based on the Resolve Issue screens. When the renewal is finalized, the system also generates the required transactions (e.g. signature code, disentitlement) based on the Resolve Issue screens. If a disentitlement or indefinite disqualification is imposed, the system creates a Correspondence WI for the D-01-00-00 letter. This means that the officer with the CA or SA WI has no action to perform for these ADJ WIs.

example_shared_block: Fraudulent paper ROEs were created without the knowledge of the true SIN-holder and the employer associated with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) business number (BN) indicated in block 5 of the ROE. There are also instances where there are reasons to suspect that the business identified on the ROE is illegitimate or suspicious and was created to issue fraudulent ROEs. These fraudulent ROEs were sent to Service Canada and scanned as documents in support of fraudulent applications for benefits, or uploaded in AW or MSCA. A close examination may reveal a difference in the font and size of the characters in the serial number of these ROEs when compared to the normal format. In some cases, RCM validates the serial number and does not signal the ROE as a duplicate, because that serial number was used to establish an EI claim more than 11 years ago. In other situations, the serial number has been issued within the last 11 years to a different business number than the one used on the fraudulent ROE, however, RCM validates the serial number but does not flag it as a duplicate because the ROE was never used to establish an EI claim.

document2: Adjudicating non-referred training: Regular or fishing benefits — Renewal claim
example_shared_block: When clients report that they are attending full-time training on their own initiative, the officer refers to BE 2023-05 — Federal Court of Appeal decision: William Page (A-29-22) and availability for students on full-time training and the Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles 10.12.2.8 — Hours of work . Both the BE Memo and the Digest explain that, under FCA A-29-22 , when adjudicating availability, the officer must consider the clients’ work history while attending training, in addition to other factors (i.e. the number of hours clients are attending training). Clients can rebut the presumption of non-availability if they can demonstrate having a regular work history outside of the training hours while taking full-time training. Using any previous ROEs, the officer reviews the number of hours the client worked while attending training to determine if the client can rebut the presumption of non-availability. Clients must also demonstrate a willingness and ability to remain available for a similar work schedule. Clients must not reduce or restrict their available hours of work beyond what is reasonable, given their work history, while attending training. example_shared_block: The employer pays the client for the first 14-calendar-day period or less, in accordance with the period of the incapacity, and is, in turn, reimbursed by the CNESST. The amount paid by the employer is 90% of the client’s net salary. These monies are considered a WCB amount and must be allocated as such. The employer’s coverage is for the equivalent number of days that the client would have normally worked during the 14-calendar-day pay period immediately following the accident or incapacity (work-related illness). The earnings are allocated based on the number of days the client would have worked in that period. After the 14-calendar-day period, the compensation is paid directly by the CNESST.

Separation monies are intended to compensate for the loss of wages and benefits related to that employment. Unless the client is able to show that the monies received on separation are not intended to compensate for the loss of wages or benefits related to the employment, the monies are considered to be earnings from employment and paid or payable on separation. Once that determination has been made, the monies are considered earnings and must be allocated.

If it is determined that the client left the employment without just cause, a disqualification is imposed on the claim for regular benefits, unless the client has worked enough insurable hours since the voluntary leaving to establish a new claim. example_shared_block: The objective of a workforce reduction program is to ensure the economic viability of a company, an organization, a firm or a plant. To remain competitive, employers may have to restructure their workforce, which could include permanently reducing the number of employees. The group covered under a workforce reduction program may be all the employees (including seasonal, temporary or on call employees) or it could be limited to a sector, a particular group of workers or a particular work site. Workforce reduction could also include as little as one employee. Employees who leave under an approved workforce reduction program have a complete severance from their employment. The details of the workforce reduction program must be documented.

example_shared_block: By law, an employer must always provide notice of a layoff to the affected employees in a timely manner. When notice cannot be given in time, an employer can pay wages in lieu of notice. Provincial legislation usually specifies the minimum amount of notice that must be given to employees. However, company policy, collective agreements and in some cases, the circumstances of the layoff can provide for a greater notice period. Employers can choose to give notice to the affected employees and have them work throughout the notice period, or release the employees immediately and pay wages in lieu of notice, or have the employees work during the notice period and pay wages in lieu of notice. In some cases, an employer can choose to pay wages in lieu of notice even if there is no requirement to do so, such as in the case of a dismissal with cause.

example_shared_block: When clients report that they are attending full-time training on their own initiative, the officer refers to BE 2023-05 — Federal Court of Appeal decision: William Page (A-29-22) and availability for students on full-time training and the Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles 10.12.2.8 — Hours of work . Both the BE Memo and the Digest explain that, under FCA A-29-22 , when adjudicating availability, the officer must consider the clients’ work history while attending training, in addition to other factors (i.e. the number of hours clients are attending training). Clients can rebut the presumption of non-availability if they can demonstrate having a regular work history outside of the training hours while taking full-time training. Using any previous ROEs, the officer reviews the number of hours the client worked while attending training to determine if the client can rebut the presumption of non-availability. Clients must also demonstrate a willingness and ability to remain available for a similar work schedule. Clients must not reduce or restrict their available hours of work beyond what is reasonable, given their work history, while attending training. If there is no existing WI for this issue, the Level 1 officer creates a Claim Review (CR) WI for each contentious issue and attempts to adjudicate the issue according to the National Policy on Levels of Decision. If it is not possible to adjudicate the issue at Level 1, the Level 1 officer reassigns the CR WI for the contentious issue to Level 2 for adjudication.
